findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the remote-less working-tree fallback impossible to hit silently in CI: e.g. have the `verify-opcert` workflow step assert that the printed trust source names `origin/main`, or fail closed on a remote-less checkout when the existing `CI`/`GITHUB_ACTIONS` environment marker is set, and add a test for it.
evidence: Plan: "no remote at all (`git remote` succeeds and prints nothing): no reviewed branch and no change under review, so the working-tree configuration is kept."
Plan: "Implement this in-process in `rebar verify-opcert`, so it holds under any CI provider or none".
Plan: "It prints the trust source to stderr." This is informational only; no step checks it.
Today `actions/checkout@v7` always configures `origin`, so the current workflow does not reach this arm. Exposure depends on other CI providers or a future checkout shape, so this is advisory.
findings.finding: The remote-less arm fails open. When `git remote` succeeds but prints nothing, the gate keeps the working-tree project config, which is the config the change controls. Only a stderr line says so. The plan's own claim is that the control 'holds under any CI provider or none'. A CI provider or checkout shape that fetches a change by URL with no named remote (a tarball checkout, `git init && git fetch <url> <ref>`, some Gerrit-triggered job layouts) would silently take this arm and let the change widen its own trust list. Nothing in the plan or workflow fails or asserts when CI lands in this arm.
findings.location: Approach → Base ref failure handling, 'no remote at all (`git remote` succeeds and prints nothing): … the working-tree configuration is kept'; Approach → 'so it holds under any CI provider or none'
scenarios: The gate is moved to a CI system that materialises the patch set with `git init` plus `git fetch <url> refs/changes/...`, leaving no named remote. The change's `rebar.toml` key is trusted for its own run, and the gate passes.
A future edit to this workflow swaps `actions/checkout` for a cached tarball. The gate falls back to the working-tree config with only a stderr note.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the default: resolve `refs/remotes/origin/main` once via `git rev-parse --verify` to a SHA, use `<sha>` for all ls-tree/show calls, and print `trust source: origin/main@<sha>:<path>` (or `empty project layer` / `working tree (no remote)`) to stderr.
evidence: "the project layer is the config committed at the base ref (`git show <ref>:<path>`)"
"decided by `git ls-tree --full-tree --name-only <ref> -- <path>`"
"It prints the trust source to stderr."
findings.finding: The plan does not say to resolve origin/main to a commit SHA once and reuse it for every `ls-tree`/`show` call. It also leaves the stderr trust-source format unspecified. Separate ref lookups can straddle a concurrent fetch, a check-then-act gap. An unspecified source line gives weak audit evidence.
findings.location: Approach (base ref; "It prints the trust source to stderr")
scenarios: ls-tree runs against one main commit and git show against a newer one after a concurrent fetch.
An operator cannot tell from CI logs which main commit supplied the trust list.
findings.suggested_fix: In `gate_config`, resolve the SHA with `git rev-parse --verify refs/remotes/origin/main^{commit}`, use it for every read, and record it in the returned `source`, which `cli()` prints.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Close the no-remote fail-open: either fail closed (exit 2) whenever the run cannot establish a reviewed base, or state exactly why a remote-less checkout can never be a CI change-under-review, and test the CI-like remote-less case.
evidence: 'Implement this in-process in `rebar verify-opcert`, so it holds under any CI provider or none'
'no remote at all (`git remote` succeeds and prints nothing): no reviewed branch and no change under review, so the working-tree configuration is kept.'

Remote-less checkouts are common in CI: `git init && git fetch <url> <sha> && git checkout FETCH_HEAD` (fetch-by-SHA shallow checkouts in Jenkins/Buildkite/custom runners), or checkouts that strip remotes after cloning.
findings.finding: The 'no remote at all' arm fails open: when `git remote` prints nothing, the gate keeps the working-tree rebar.toml. A CI provider or custom pipeline that checks out without a named remote then runs the vulnerable pre-fix behavior. A change adding its own key to rebar.toml widens its own gate run, and the gate exits 0.
findings.location: Approach > Failure handling > 'no remote at all (`git remote` succeeds and prints nothing): ... the working-tree configuration is kept'
scenarios: CI under a non-GitHub provider (e.g. Jenkins or Buildkite with a fetch-by-URL/SHA checkout) has no configured remote. The PR adds `trusted_opcert_keys = ["attacker"]` to rebar.toml. `git remote` prints nothing, the gate uses the PR's rebar.toml, and it reports the attacker-signed ticket as trusted (exit 0).
The premise 'no remote ⇒ no change under review' is false in CI. The change under review is the checked-out tree whether or not a remote is named.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that `gate_config` runs its `git remote` / rev-parse / `ls-tree` / `show` calls through the existing bounded helpers (`git_fetch.git_run` + `_raise_if_timed_out`, `git_fetch.rev_parse`, or `gitutil.run_git`) and add a 'git timed out → ConfigError, exit 2' arm to the failure list.
evidence: Plan: "`git remote` exits non-zero ... `ConfigError`"; "no remote at all (`git remote` succeeds and prints nothing) ... the working-tree configuration is kept"; "the path is absent at the ref (decided by `git ls-tree --full-tree --name-only <ref> -- <path>` ...): fall through"
src/rebar/_snapshot/git_fetch.py:113-128 `git_run` (bounded) and `_raise_if_timed_out`: 'its empty output answers nothing'
src/rebar/_snapshot/git_fetch.py:140-155 `rev_parse` already resolves a ref with `--end-of-options` and treats a timeout as an error rather than unresolved
src/rebar/_snapshot/repo_snapshot.py:264-269 `_list_submodules` shows the existing `git_run(...'ls-tree'...)` + timeout check pattern
src/rebar/_store/compat.py:274 `run_git(..., "show", f"{remote_ref}:{COMPAT_FILENAME}", check=False)`
findings.finding: The plan lists the git commands `gate_config` runs (`git remote`, resolving `refs/remotes/origin/main`, `git ls-tree --full-tree --name-only`, `git show <ref>:<path>`) but doesn't say they go through the repo's bounded git helpers. `_snapshot/git_fetch.py` already has `git_run` (watchdog-bounded), `rev_parse` (`--verify --quiet --end-of-options`) and `_raise_if_timed_out`. `_store/gitutil.run_git` is the common runner used by other `git show <ref>:<path>` callers (`_store/compat.py:274`, `_commands/reclaim_publish.py:108`). None of the plan's failure arms covers a timed-out git child. A fresh `subprocess.run` would rebuild that bounding and could read a killed process's empty stdout as 'no remote' or 'path absent', which falls through to the working-tree config or an empty project layer.
findings.location: Approach → Base ref / failure-handling arms
scenarios: A slow CI runner, or a `git` hung on a credential helper, has its `git remote` or `ls-tree` killed by the watchdog. Empty stdout plus an unchecked timeout lands in the 'no remote' or 'path absent' arm, and the gate keeps the working-tree config or an empty project layer, which is the bypass the plan is closing.
findings.suggested_fix: In the failure-handling list, add: 'any git call killed by its watchdog (`is_watchdog_timeout`) → `ConfigError`, exit 2'. Also name `rebar._snapshot.git_fetch.git_run` / `rev_parse` as the runners. Note that `has_remote` itself is unsuitable, because it ignores a non-zero exit, which is why the plan needs its own `git remote` check.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Close the no-remote arm or narrow it: either fail closed (exit 2) when no reviewed base can be resolved, or keep the fallback but limit the 'any CI provider' claim to checkouts with an `origin` remote and have each gating CI lane assert the printed trust source is `origin/main`.
evidence: Plan: "no remote at all (`git remote` succeeds and prints nothing): no reviewed branch and no change under review, so the working-tree configuration is kept."
Plan: "Implement this in-process in `rebar verify-opcert`, so it holds under any CI provider or none"
verify-identity.yml header: "Gerrit verifies each patch set before merge". So a second, non-GitHub lane runs the gate, and nothing in the plan says how its checkout is prepared.
findings.finding: The no-remote fallback ('`git remote` succeeds and prints nothing … the working-tree configuration is kept') trusts the working tree with no check. It assumes that a checkout without a remote has no change under review. That contradicts the Approach's stated goal that the fix 'holds under any CI provider or none'. Some CI systems prepare checkouts without an `origin` remote, for example a Gerrit-driven merger or a `git init` followed by a fetch by URL. Under those, the gate silently reads the change's own `rebar.toml`, which is exactly the attack the plan exists to close. The only signal is a trust-source line on stderr.
findings.location: Approach — Base ref failure handling, 'no remote at all' arm; Approach intro 'so it holds under any CI provider or none'
scenarios: A Gerrit or other non-GitHub CI lane prepares the change in a repository with no remotes. `gate_config` returns the working-tree layer, and a patch set that adds its own key to `rebar.toml` passes its own gate.
A CI job runs `git remote remove origin` or clones with `--origin` set to another name. Another name is caught: remote exists, `origin/main` missing, exit 2. Removing every remote is not caught.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Acknowledge the behavior change for local and non-`main`-default consumers in docs/exit-codes.md or the changelog, and state the back-out (revert the commit; consumers can create `refs/remotes/origin/main`).
evidence: "Base ref: `refs/remotes/origin/main` only"
"a remote exists but `origin/main` does not resolve: `ConfigError`, exit 2"
"The gate runs under `local_read_context()` ... the gate verifies the store as mounted"
No statement about local or non-CI usage, non-main default branches, or rollback.
findings.finding: The plan changes existing behavior for every non-CI invocation without acknowledging it or giving a back-out path. A local developer with an origin remote now gets origin/main's (possibly stale) config, not their working tree. Their uncommitted rebar.toml edits are ignored. The store no longer read-time syncs under local_read_context. Consumer repos whose default branch is not `main` (or whose remote is not `origin`) now always exit 2.
findings.location: Approach (base ref / failure arms / local_read_context); Out of scope
scenarios: A repo using `master` or `trunk` upgrades rebar and every `rebar verify-opcert` exits 2.
A developer edits trusted_opcert_keys locally to test and sees no effect, with no indication beyond the stderr source line.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Address non-`main`/non-`origin` repositories: either justify restricting verify-opcert to `origin/main` repos and document that requirement in manifest-signing.md and exit-codes.md, or derive the reviewed ref (e.g. `refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`) without adding a working-tree-controllable knob.
evidence: 'Base ref: `refs/remotes/origin/main` only'
'a remote exists but `origin/main` does not resolve: `ConfigError`, exit 2, naming the `git fetch` that fixes it'
Docs scope includes consumer-facing docs (`docs/manifest-signing.md`, `docs/plan-review-gate.md`, `docs/cli-reference.md`), so verify-opcert is shipped to target projects, not only rebar's own repo.
findings.finding: Hardcoding `refs/remotes/origin/main` breaks the gate in two kinds of repository. In repos whose integration branch is not `main` (e.g. `master`, `trunk`), every run exits 2 with a misleading `git fetch` hint. In checkouts whose remote is not named `origin`, the plan's arm 'a remote exists but origin/main does not resolve → ConfigError exit 2' also fires on every run. The plan offers no way out, since 'the base ref is fixed at origin/main'.
findings.location: Approach > 'Base ref: `refs/remotes/origin/main` only' / 'No config key, env var or flag is added: the base ref is fixed at `origin/main`.'
scenarios: A developer workstation or CI run in a consumer project whose default branch is `master` (common in older Ruby/Java/.NET repos) gets exit 2 on every `rebar verify-opcert`. The suggested `git fetch origin` cannot create `origin/main`.
A GitLab CI or Jenkins job whose git plugin names the remote something other than `origin` (a remote exists, `origin/main` is absent) fails exit 2 permanently.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Document the order a trust-list change requires (merge the new key to main before the environment signs with it) and the recovery when a cert from an unlisted key is already closed. Add this to `docs/manifest-signing.md` and the runbook alongside the enforcement-flip note.
evidence: verify_opcert.py:148-151: `events = _collect_all(tracker)` … `ticket_ids = sorted({ev.ticket_id for ev in events if ev.ticket_id})`. Every closed ticket in the store is in scope, not just the change's.
Plan: "`infra/runbooks/mcp-opcert-enforcement-flip.md` (an enforcement flip takes effect after it merges, not in its own gate run)". Only the flip is covered, not adding or rotating a key.
Plan Testing: "exit 1 `untrusted` before merge, exit 0 after". This is the same behaviour that blocks a legitimate key-addition PR.
findings.finding: Under the new design, a trust-list change can block itself. The gate walks every closed ticket in the shared `tickets` store (`ticket_ids` comes from all events in `_collect_all(tracker)`), and it now judges them against main's list. Suppose an environment starts signing completion certs with a new or rotated key, and an enforced ticket is closed with it before the PR adding that key merges. Then that PR's own gate run fails (`untrusted`, exit 1), and so does every other PR, until the PR merges by bypassing the gate. Under the old behaviour the PR adding the key passed its own run. The plan updates the runbook only for the enforcement flip and never states the required order (merge the key to main before the environment signs with it) or the recovery path.
findings.location: Approach — Docs bullet (`infra/runbooks/mcp-opcert-enforcement-flip.md`); `src/rebar/_commands/verify_opcert.py` ticket walk
scenarios: An operator rotates the CI environment's op-cert key. A ticket closes with a cert from the new key before the `rebar.toml` PR lands. Every PR, including the one adding the key, fails `verify-opcert` until someone overrides the gate.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to `docs/manifest-signing.md` and `infra/runbooks/mcp-opcert-enforcement-flip.md`: 'Adding or rotating a key in `verify.trusted_opcert_keys` takes effect only once it is on main, so merge the key before the environment signs with it. If an enforced ticket already carries a cert from an unlisted key, every gate run fails until the key is on main; land it through <named override path>.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that `bind_operation_snapshot` is used as a scoped context (with `local_read_context()`) and released in `finally`, and add a test asserting the snapshot is unbound after `cli()` returns or raises.
evidence: "returned as an `OperationSnapshot` ... and bound for the run with `bind_operation_snapshot`."
"A test runs the gate in-process from the fixture repo"
findings.finding: The OperationSnapshot is bound "for the run", but the plan gives no unbind/cleanup scope. The gate is explicitly run in-process in tests. A binding that is not reset leaks main's config into later in-process callers and other tests.
findings.location: Approach (OperationSnapshot paragraph)
scenarios: A later test in the same pytest process calls `config.tracker_dir` and gets the previous fixture's main tracker.dir.
A future in-process caller (MCP server) runs the gate and keeps a stale snapshot.
findings.suggested_fix: In `cli()`, do `with bind_operation_snapshot(snapshot), local_read_context(): ...`, or use an explicit token reset in a `finally` block. Add an assertion in the in-process test that the snapshot is unbound after the call.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the test also record every working-tree discovery call site and assert the only one reached is the allowed cross-session warning path, in addition to asserting the `untrusted` verdict.
evidence: "makes every working-tree project-config discovery raise `AssertionError` (not `ConfigError`, which `_sync_disabled` would swallow)"
"`_lib_warn.emit_cross_session_warning` swallows every error"
findings.finding: The in-process test makes working-tree discovery raise AssertionError and then asserts main's verdict. The plan already accepts that one read (the cross-session warning) swallows the error. Any other reader that catches broadly and falls back to defaults would also hide a working-tree read, and the verdict could still coincidentally match.

It also does not say which disposition wins in the fall-through chain (rebar.toml → pyproject.toml → empty layer → working-tree fallback). findings.finding: The plan changes behavior for existing callers but acknowledges only some of them. (a) A developer running `rebar verify-opcert` locally now gets the trust list from a possibly stale local `origin/main` instead of their checkout's rebar.toml. The plan scopes out 'keeping … the gate's code and the workflow file out of the change's reach', yet `.github/workflows/verify-identity.yml` runs `pip install -e .` on the change's own checkout and then `rebar verify-opcert`. findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Say which existing `rebar._snapshot.git_fetch` primitives `gate_config` reuses (`git_run`/`run_git_bounded` with timeout, `rev_parse`), state that `has_remote` must NOT be used because it treats a non-zero `git remote` as 'no remote', and add a bounded-timeout → ConfigError/exit 2 arm for every git call, including the lazily fetching `git show`.
evidence: Plan: '`git remote` exits non-zero (not a repository, safe.directory refusal): `ConfigError`, exit 2; no remote at all (`git remote` succeeds and prints nothing) ... the working-tree configuration is kept.'

src/rebar/_snapshot/git_fetch.py:131-137: `has_remote` runs `git_run(repo_root, "remote")`, checks only for a watchdog timeout, then returns `remote in remotes` from stdout without checking returncode. A failing `git remote` therefore reads as 'absent'.

src/rebar/_snapshot/git_fetch.py:113-128, 140-155: `git_run` uses `run_git_bounded(..., timeout=_GIT_TIMEOUT)`, and `rev_parse` raises SnapshotError on timeout rather than returning None. This is the repo's established fail-closed git pattern.
The plan does not mention git timeouts, `run_git_bounded`, `rev_parse`, or `has_remote`.
findings.finding: The new `_opcert_gate_config.py` adds its own git plumbing (`git remote`, ref resolution, `ls-tree`, `git show`). The plan never mentions the bounded git primitives the repo already has, or says why it reuses or avoids each one. The closest existing helper, `rebar._snapshot.git_fetch.has_remote`, ignores the return code. A non-zero `git remote` therefore produces empty stdout and returns False ('no remote'). In this gate that is the fail-open arm that keeps the working-tree config, exactly what the plan's 'git remote exits non-zero → ConfigError' arm forbids. The plan also gives no timeout for the new git calls. The existing primitives (`git_run` → `run_git_bounded`, `_raise_if_timed_out`, `rev_parse`) fail closed on a watchdog timeout. A blobless `git show` can lazy-fetch over the network, so leaving it unbounded can hang the CI gate.
findings.location: Approach → `gate_config(root)` / Base ref failure handling; src/rebar/_snapshot/git_fetch.py
scenarios: An implementer reuses `has_remote(root)` for the 'no remote' arm. On a safe.directory refusal it returns False and the gate silently falls back to the change's own rebar.toml, which reopens the attack.
In CI, `git show refs/remotes/origin/main:rebar.toml` triggers a lazy promisor fetch that stalls. An unbounded subprocess hangs the gate until the job timeout instead of exiting 2 with a diagnostic.
findings.suggested_fix: In the Approach's failure-handling list, add one line: "All git calls go through `rebar._snapshot.git_fetch.git_run` (bounded by `_GIT_TIMEOUT`). A watchdog timeout on `git remote`, `rev-parse`, `ls-tree` or `git show` raises `ConfigError`, exit 2. `has_remote` is not used because it ignores `git remote`'s exit status; `gate_config` checks the returncode itself to separate 'non-zero' (exit 2) from 'succeeded, empty' (no remote)." Add a timeout case to tests/unit/test_opcert_gate_config.py.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In the Base ref section, compare the fixed `origin/main` choice with base-branch resolution (the CODEOWNERS model): either state that main is the sole trust authority for all branches this workflow runs on (and why a hard-coded ref beats an attacker-uncontrollable base ref such as `GITHUB_BASE_REF`), or scope the workflow/gate to PRs and pushes whose target is main.
evidence: Plan: 'Base ref: `refs/remotes/origin/main` only, the ref attested gates already treat as reviewed main (`rebar.llm.gate_source.DEFAULT_REF`...)'.
src/rebar/llm/gate_source.py:73-77: the attested gates' `default_ref()` resolves `REBAR_GATE_REF` > `[snapshot].ref` > `origin/main`, so for them origin/main is only the default.
.github/workflows/verify-identity.yml:11-18: triggers are `push` (branches-ignore feature/**, main, tickets), `pull_request: {}`, `workflow_dispatch`, `schedule`.

Prior art: per Google Cloud's Secure Source Manager docs, <cite index="2-1">the system uses only CODEOWNERS files from the base branch (the branch you are merging into) to determine approval requirements.</cite>
Prior art: <cite index="8-1">the copy that governs a pull request is the one on the base branch, so an ownership change never applies to the pull request that makes it.</cite>
findings.finding: The plan fixes the trusted ref at `refs/remotes/origin/main`. It never compares this with the established approach for 'config that governs a change is read from the reviewed branch', which is the PR's base branch (the branch being merged into), as with CODEOWNERS. verify-identity.yml runs on `pull_request: {}` for any base, and on pushes to every branch except `feature/**`, `main` and `tickets`. For a PR targeting another branch (e.g. a release or integration branch), the gate would judge the change against main's trust list and `require_environment`, not the target branch's. The plan's only justification is consistency with the attested gates' DEFAULT_REF, which those gates treat as an overridable default.
findings.location: Approach → 'Base ref: `refs/remotes/origin/main` only'; 'No config key, env var or flag is added: the base ref is fixed at `origin/main`.'
scenarios: A PR targets `release/x`, which legitimately has a different trust list or enforcement posture from main. The gate applies main's config, producing a false `untrusted` failure or a weaker/stronger posture than the target branch intends.
A push to a non-main, non-feature branch has no PR base. Nothing says main is the intended policy authority for that branch.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that the gate's `git show origin/main:<path>` lazily fetches main's config blob in the blobless CI clone (needs network, persisted checkout credentials, and no `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH`), or have the workflow step materialize the blob before `rebar verify-opcert` runs, and say which.
evidence: Plan: "the `verify-opcert` step fetches `refs/heads/main` into `refs/remotes/origin/main` (blobless, after the pack measurement) before running the gate."

Plan failure arm: "`git show` of a listed path fails (for example a blobless clone cannot fetch the blob) ... `ConfigError`, exit 2". Lazy fetch is described only as a failure mode, not as a precondition of the normal path.
`.github/workflows/verify-identity.yml:52-56`: `actions/checkout@v7` with `filter: blob:none`, `fetch-depth: 1`. The clone is a promisor partial clone, so missing blobs are fetched lazily on demand.

Repo precedent for disabling lazy fetch: `src/rebar/_snapshot/git_fetch.py:171` sets `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1`. If gate_config's git calls reuse a helper or environment like that, `git show` cannot fetch main's blob.

Evidence class: Partially-verified. Partial-clone lazy fetch is a real git capability, but the plan does not state the auth, network and env preconditions the gate step needs, and I could not observe them.
findings.finding: The plan fetches main blobless, so main's `rebar.toml` blob (which differs from the change's copy in exactly the attack case) is not in the object database when `rebar verify-opcert` runs `git show refs/remotes/origin/main:<path>`. The happy path therefore depends on git lazily fetching that blob from the promisor remote during the gate step. That needs network access, the credentials `actions/checkout` persists, and no `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH` in the subprocess environment. The plan states none of these. It mentions lazy fetching only as a failure arm ("a blobless clone cannot fetch the blob" → exit 2). If the lazy fetch is suppressed or unauthenticated, every CI run fails closed with exit 2 instead of reaching a verdict.
findings.location: Approach — `.github/workflows/verify-identity.yml` bullet ("fetches `refs/heads/main` into `refs/remotes/origin/main` (blobless, after the pack measurement)") and the `git show` failure arm
scenarios: A PR edits `rebar.toml` to add its own key. Main's `rebar.toml` blob is not present locally, `git show` triggers a lazy fetch, and the job's checkout credentials (persisted by default) must still be valid at the gate step.

A later hardening sets `persist-credentials: false` on checkout, or gate_config runs git with `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1`. `git show` then fails on every run, the gate exits 2, and the CI lane is permanently red with a config-error message instead of a verdict.
An offline or self-hosted runner without network at gate time hits the same unconditional exit 2.
findings.suggested_fix: In the `verify-opcert` step, after `git fetch --filter=blob:none --no-tags origin +refs/heads/main:refs/remotes/origin/main`, run `git cat-file -e refs/remotes/origin/main:rebar.toml || true` so the blob is fetched while the step's credentials are known to be in place. Then document in the plan that gate_config runs `git show` without `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH`, so a missing blob is either fetched lazily or fails closed (exit 2).

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Name the control that keeps the gate's code, the workflow file and the user/env layers out of the change's reach in the `verify-opcert` lane (a ticket or an existing mechanism, e.g. running the gate from a main-pinned install), or reword AC 1 and the doc updates to say the property holds only when that control is in place.
evidence: Plan: "keeping it, the gate's code and the workflow file out of the change's reach is the CI lane's job" — no ticket, ADR or existing control is named.
verify-identity.yml lines 101-104: `python -m pip install -e .` installs the checked-out change's rebar before the `verify-opcert` step (line 132-135).
verify-identity.yml line 17: `pull_request: {}` — the workflow definition is taken from the change's merge ref.
Plan AC: "The CI op-cert gate reads `verify.trusted_opcert_keys` from main's committed `rebar.toml`, not the change's" — stated as a CI property, but it only holds while the gate code is trusted.
findings.finding: The plan's control runs inside code and a workflow that the lower-trust actor controls in the lane the plan edits. The plan hands that protection to 'the CI lane' without naming any control, yet its first acceptance criterion claims the CI gate reads main's trust list. In `.github/workflows/verify-identity.yml` the change's own package is installed with `python -m pip install -e .` before `rebar verify-opcert` runs. That install runs the change's build backend and installs the change's version of `_opcert_gate_config.py` and `verify_opcert.py`. On `pull_request` the workflow file itself also comes from the change. A hostile change can therefore edit `gate_config` itself, or write the user config layer or `$GITHUB_ENV` (both still composed by `gate_config`), and get past the new check. Only a change that does not touch these files is actually stopped.
findings.location: Approach → 'Out of scope: … keeping it, the gate's code and the workflow file out of the change's reach is the CI lane's job'; Acceptance Criteria item 1; .github/workflows/verify-identity.yml 'Install rebar' step
scenarios: A change edits `src/rebar/_opcert_gate_config.py` to return the working-tree config along with its own `rebar.toml` key. Its own `verify-opcert` run installs that code with `pip install -e .` and passes.

A change sets a custom in-tree build backend in `pyproject.toml` that writes `~/.config/rebar/config.toml` or appends `REBAR_*` lines to `$GITHUB_ENV` during `pip install`. `gate_config` still composes the user and environment layers.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a sentence to Out of scope and to the doc updates naming the residual risk (`pip install -e .` installs the change's gate code, and pull_request runs the change's workflow) and linking a follow-up ticket. Scope AC 1 to 'given a trusted gate binary', or have the workflow step install rebar from `origin/main` (e.g. `git worktree add` of origin/main, then `pip install` from it) before running the gate.

metrics.claim_path: no-llm/no-network (structural; the fast claim check is a local HMAC verify)
